title: Situational Awareness Fundamentals
summary: Learn to notice trouble early so you can step away from it long before it reaches you. Use this every day, and especially after a disaster when normal order is strained.

steps.title: Look up from your phone
steps.body: The single biggest awareness killer is a screen. When you walk through a parking lot, a crowded store, a fuel line, or a shelter, keep the phone in your pocket unless you are standing still with your back to a wall. If you need to read or text, stop, step to the side, and glance up every few seconds. Wear only one earbud, or none, in public places after a disaster. You cannot react to a car backing toward you, a fight starting, or a crowd surging if you never see it begin. Most people who say 'it came out of nowhere' were looking down.

steps.title: Use a simple alertness dial
steps.body: Many trainers use a color scale. White means tuned out - fine at home behind locked doors, risky anywhere else. Yellow means relaxed but aware: you notice who is around you and where the exits are. This is your normal setting in public, and you can hold it all day without stress. Orange means something specific caught your attention, so you watch it and decide what you will do if it gets worse. Red means it got worse and you are acting on your plan - leaving, getting to staff, or calling 911. The goal is to spend your time in Yellow so you reach Orange early, while leaving is still easy.

steps.title: Learn the baseline of a place
steps.body: Every place has a normal rhythm. At a distribution site, people wait in line, chat, and look tired. At a gas station, people pump fuel and leave. In your first 30 seconds anywhere, take in that normal picture: how many people, how loud it is, where staff stand, where the doors are. Once you know what normal looks like, things that do not fit stand out on their own. You are not looking for bad people; you are looking for changes - a sudden hush, raised voices, people drifting away from one spot, or someone who keeps circling the parking lot instead of doing business.

steps.title: Watch behavior, not appearance
steps.body: Judge actions, never race, religion, clothing style, or age. DHS lists behaviors worth noticing, such as unusual interest in security, people trying to enter restricted areas or posing as staff, and asking detailed questions that go beyond normal curiosity. In daily life, useful signs include someone watching you or your vehicle rather than the scene, a person who keeps closing distance after you move away, two or more people who seem to coordinate while pretending not to know each other, and anger that keeps rising. One odd behavior means little. A cluster of them, getting stronger, means it is time to act.

steps.title: Know your exits and make a what-if plan
steps.body: When you settle anywhere - a restaurant, a shelter cot, a waiting room - note at least two ways out, including ones staff use. Sit where you can see the main entrance if you can. Then quietly ask yourself, 'If something went wrong right now, where would I go?' This takes five seconds and means you will not freeze later. With family, agree on simple words like 'we're leaving' that mean move now and ask questions later. Children can learn this as a game: point out the exits when you walk into a store.

steps.title: Act early and choose distance
steps.body: When your gut says something is wrong, trust it and leave early. Walking away from a tense line or crossing the street costs you a few minutes; waiting to be sure can cost much more. Move toward people who can help - staff, security, police, or a busy lighted area. Do not stay to watch a fight or argument, and do not record it up close. If someone follows you, go into an open business, not toward your home or car, and call 911. Leaving is not cowardice. It is the safest choice almost every time.

steps.title: Report what you saw
steps.body: If something seems wrong, tell someone with authority: local police, shelter staff, or site security. Call 911 if anyone is in danger right now. Give the basic facts - who you saw, what they did, when, where, and why it seemed off. Stick to what you observed, not guesses. Describe the person by clothing, height, direction of travel, and any vehicle and plate. Reporting is how officials connect small pieces into a bigger picture, and it lets trained people handle the situation instead of you.

warnings: Awareness is not suspicion of whole groups. Profiling by race, religion, or appearance is wrong and leads you to miss real warning signs.
Never follow, confront, or try to detain someone you think is suspicious. Observe from a safe distance and report.
Constant fear is exhausting and makes judgment worse. Relaxed alertness (Yellow) is the goal, not nonstop high alert.
If someone is in immediate danger, call 911 first and observe second.
proTips: Practice in normal life: in each store, name the exits and one thing that would look out of place there. It becomes automatic within a few weeks.
Park facing out and near a light when you can, so leaving is quick and you can see the area around your car.
Use reflections in windows and glass doors to check behind you without turning around.
Agree on a family code word that means 'leave now, no questions.'
source: DHS 'If You See Something, Say Something' / CISA de-escalation guidance

sources.title: Recognize the Signs of Suspicious Activity

whenNotTo: Do not use 'awareness' as a reason to watch, follow, or photograph a person who has done nothing wrong.
If danger is already happening (shots, fire, a fight moving toward you), skip the analysis and leave - see fm-004 and sec-010.

quickGlance.situation: You are out in public after a disaster - lines, crowds, fuel stops, shelters - and want to spot trouble early enough to avoid it.
immediate: Put the phone away and look around
Note two exits wherever you stop
Watch for changes in behavior, not appearance
If something feels wrong, leave early toward help
then: Report what you saw to police or staff - call 911 if anyone is in danger
Practice exit-spotting daily so it becomes habit

title: Home Perimeter Awareness and Early Warning
summary: Set up simple, legal layers around your home - clear sightlines, lighting, alarms, and neighbors - so you get early warning of anyone approaching and have time to lock up and call for help.

steps.title: Think in layers
steps.body: Good home security is a set of layers, each one buying a little time. The outer layer is your street and neighbors who notice strangers. The middle layer is your yard: clear sightlines, lighting, and a fence or gate that shows where private property begins. The inner layer is the house itself: solid doors, locks, and window security. The last layer is your plan: a safe room, a phone, and a way out. No single layer stops everything, but together they make your home a poor target and give you warning. The goal is never to fight anyone - it is to notice early, stay inside, and get help.

steps.title: Walk your property like a stranger
steps.body: In daylight and again after dark, walk slowly around your home from the street. Ask where someone could hide, which doors and windows cannot be seen from the street or a neighbor's house, and which paths lead to the back without being noticed. Police crime-prevention programs call this natural surveillance. Write down every blind spot. Typical problems are tall shrubs under windows, a dark side yard, a gate that does not latch, ladders or tools left outside, and a garage left open. Fixing these costs little and matters more than any gadget.

steps.title: Open up sightlines and add light
steps.body: Trim shrubs near the house to about 2 feet (0.6 m) and prune low tree branches up to about 6 feet (1.8 m) so neighbors and passersby can see your doors and windows. Light every entrance, walkway, and parking area. Motion-sensor lights on the sides and back of the house are cheap and work well; solar or battery models keep working when the grid is down. Bright white light is better than dim yellow in dark corners. Keep house numbers large and lighted so police, fire, and EMS can find you fast.

steps.title: Add simple early-warning devices
steps.body: Battery-powered door and window alarms, wireless driveway chimes, and a video doorbell all tell you someone is close before they reach the door. Choose devices that run on batteries or have battery backup, and keep spare batteries. A dog that barks at strangers is one of the best warnings there is. Inside, keep a flashlight and charged phone by the bed. When a device alerts, do not go outside to check. Turn on lights, lock up, look from a window, and call 911 if someone is trying to get in.

steps.title: Never use traps or hazards
steps.body: Do not set trip lines across paths, hidden pits, spikes, or anything meant to hurt a person. Booby traps are illegal in the United States even on your own land, and they injure the wrong people: children, neighbors, firefighters, EMS crews, and you. Courts have held owners responsible for injuries from traps. Any early warning you use should make light or sound only and should be placed where nobody will trip on it, such as a chime on a gate or an alarm on a door.

steps.title: Use your neighbors as the outer layer
steps.body: The best perimeter is a street where people know each other. Trade phone numbers with neighbors, agree to watch each other's homes, and tell each other when you will be away. After a disaster, neighbors who check on each other notice strangers, spot fires, and help the elderly. A formal neighborhood watch makes this stronger; see sec-012. If you need a night watch during a long outage, keep it at home, in pairs, and built around calling for help, not patrolling.

warnings: Never build traps or devices that can injure. They are illegal and often hurt children or emergency responders.
Do not go outside to investigate an alarm or a noise at night. Lock up, turn on lights, and call 911.
Never run a generator or grill in a garage or near windows to keep lights on - carbon monoxide kills. Keep generators at least 20 feet from the home.
Do not block doors or windows you may need to escape a fire.
proTips: Solar motion lights with a separate panel can be placed in shade and still charge, and they keep working in long outages.
Keep your yard looking cared for during a crisis. Mowed grass and picked-up trash signal that someone is home and paying attention.
Gravel paths near windows make footsteps easy to hear.
Many police departments offer free home security surveys. Ask your local crime-prevention officer.
source: Local police CPTED programs (Liberty MO, Menlo Park CA)

sources.title: Start a Neighborhood Watch
sources.publisher: National Neighborhood Watch Institute / National Sheriffs' Association

whenNotTo: Do not rely on perimeter measures when officials order an evacuation - leave.
Do not use alarms or lights as a reason to confront anyone outside.

quickGlance.situation: You want early warning of anyone approaching your home, especially during a long outage.
immediate: Walk the property and list blind spots
Trim shrubs to about 2 ft and tree limbs up to about 6 ft
Add battery or solar motion lights and door alarms
then: Trade numbers with neighbors and watch each other's homes
If an alarm goes off at night, stay inside, lock up, and call 911

title: Evacuation Planning: When and How to Leave
summary: Build a plan to leave home quickly and safely - where you will go, how you will get there, what you will take, and the signals that tell you it is time. Make it before you need it.

steps.title: Decide when you would stay and when you would go
steps.body: Staying home is usually safer when your home is undamaged and not in the hazard's path, because you have your supplies and shelter. Leave when officials order an evacuation, when the hazard is coming toward you (wildfire, flood, storm surge, chemical release), when your home is no longer safe, or when someone in the household needs care you cannot provide there. Write down your personal triggers ahead of time, such as 'if the fire reaches the ridge' or 'if we lose water and the road might close.' Deciding in advance keeps you from waiting too long, which is the most common mistake.

steps.title: Learn your local alert levels
steps.body: Many counties use a three-step system. In Oregon's version, Level 1 'Be Ready' means stay alert and check your go bag. Level 2 'Be Set' means danger is close - leave now if you need extra time because of mobility needs, large animals, or a long drive. Level 3 'Go Now' means leave immediately without gathering belongings. Other areas use Ready-Set-Go or evacuation zones; look up yours and sign up for your county's emergency alerts and Wireless Emergency Alerts on your phone. Only go back home after an official all-clear.

steps.title: Pick destinations before you need them
steps.body: Choose at least two places to go: one nearby (a friend or relative across town, outside the hazard area) and one farther away (out of the region). Ask these hosts ahead of time and agree on how you will contact them. Know where public shelters typically open in your area, and remember that most shelters cannot take pets, so line up a pet-friendly option. A destination like 'somewhere safer' is not a plan. Write the addresses down on paper in your go bag in case your phone dies.

steps.title: Map more than one route
steps.body: For each destination, plan a main route and at least one backup that uses different roads and bridges. Download offline maps and keep a paper road map, because cell service often fails. Note choke points such as bridges, tunnels, and low roads that flood. Follow routes officials announce - they may close roads or change lanes - and never drive around barricades. Never drive into floodwater; a foot of moving water can float many vehicles. Keep your tank at least half full during the season of your local hazard.

steps.title: Pack a go bag for each person
steps.body: A practical go bag holds: water (1 gallon per person per day for at least 3 days), 3 days of non-perishable food, a 7-day supply of medicines and copies of prescriptions, copies of ID, insurance, and deed or lease, a phone charger and backup battery, a first aid kit, a flashlight and spare batteries, cash in small bills, a change of clothes, N95 masks where wildfire smoke is a risk, and pet food, carrier, and records. Add comfort items for children and older adults. Keep bags light enough that each person can carry their own.

steps.title: Leave early and tell someone
steps.body: When it is time, confirm the alert came from an official source, grab go bags, load pets, and take medications. Text your out-of-area contact that you are leaving and where you are headed - texts get through when calls do not. Lock up and leave a light on so responders can tell the home is empty if local guidance says to. Take your planned route and do not wait for traffic to clear. Leaving early beats every other tactic: roads are open, fuel is available, and you are not making decisions in panic.

steps.title: Practice once a year
steps.body: Run your evacuation once a year as a family drill. Time how long it takes to get everyone, the pets, and the bags into the car. Most families are surprised at how long it takes the first time. Update bag contents with the seasons, swap out food and water before it expires, refresh medicines, and check that children's clothes still fit. Make sure every adult knows the destinations and routes, not just one person.

warnings: Never drive around road barricades or into floodwater. Turn around and find another route.
Do not wait until a hazard is visible to leave. By then roads may be jammed or closed.
Do not return home until officials say the area is safe.
An overloaded bag you cannot carry is worse than a light one. Pack for what you can actually move.
proTips: Keep a printed list taped inside a closet door of last-minute items to grab: meds from the fridge, chargers, glasses, pet carrier.
Store a small go bag in your vehicle as a backup in case you must leave from work or school.
Photograph each room before you leave - it helps with insurance claims later.
Share your plan with your out-of-area contact so someone outside the disaster knows where to look for you.
source: Linn County (OR) Sheriff evacuation guidance / Ready.gov

sources.title: Family Emergency Communication Plan
sources.publisher: Oklahoma Emergency Management (Ready.gov template), hosted by NJ OEM

whenNotTo: Do not evacuate into the path of a hazard - for a tornado warning, take shelter where you are instead.
If officials tell you to shelter in place (for example, a chemical release), stay inside unless told otherwise.

quickGlance.situation: A hazard is threatening your area and you may need to leave home quickly.
immediate: Confirm the alert is official and know your alert level
Grab go bags, medicines, and pets
Text your out-of-area contact where you are going
Leave early by your planned route - never drive into floodwater
then: Check in when you arrive
Return only after the official all-clear

title: Hardening Your Home: Doors, Windows, Lighting, and Visibility
summary: Make your home a harder, less attractive target with low-cost upgrades to doors, windows, lighting, and landscaping, based on police crime-prevention (CPTED) guidance. Do this before a disaster, when hardware stores are open.

steps.title: Understand the three CPTED ideas
steps.body: Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design (CPTED) is the approach police departments use for home security reviews. It rests on three ideas. Natural surveillance: make your doors and windows easy for neighbors and passersby to see. Territorial reinforcement: use fences, paths, porches, and upkeep to show clearly where private property begins and that someone cares for it. Access control: guide visitors to the front door and make other ways in harder. Most burglars look for an easy, hidden, unoccupied target. Each upgrade below takes away one of those.

steps.title: Upgrade exterior doors
steps.body: Use solid-core wood or metal exterior doors; hollow doors break easily. Install a deadbolt whose bolt extends at least 1 inch (2.5 cm) into the frame. The weak point is usually the frame, not the lock: replace the short screws in the strike plate with 3 to 4 inch (7.5 to 10 cm) wood screws that reach the wall stud, or install a heavy-duty four-screw strike plate. Put at least one long screw in each hinge too. If glass is within reach of the lock, follow your local code on lock type, since double-cylinder locks can slow a fire escape. Add a deadbolt on the door between the garage and the house.

steps.title: Secure windows and sliding doors
steps.body: Lock every window, including upper floors reachable from a porch roof or fence. Add pin locks or secondary locks to windows that can be pried. For a sliding glass door, place a cut-to-fit bar or dowel in the bottom track and add an anti-lift device or screws in the upper track so the panel cannot be lifted out. Security film can make glass harder to break through quickly. Keep valuables out of view from windows. Most important: every bedroom must still have a window or door that opens quickly from inside for fire escape. If you install bars, use ones with a quick-release latch inside.

steps.title: Light it up
steps.body: Light every doorway, walkway, driveway, and parking spot. Use bright white light for dark corners and side yards, and place lights where trees will not block them. Motion-sensor lights startle people and alert you. During outages, solar motion lights and battery puck lights keep working. Inside, use timers or smart plugs on lamps when you are away so the house looks occupied. Avoid glare that blinds neighbors or creates deep shadows next to bright spots - even, steady light beats one blinding floodlight.

steps.title: Trim landscaping and improve sightlines
steps.body: Trim shrubs to about 2 feet (0.6 m) and prune tree branches up to about 6 feet (1.8 m) off the ground, especially near doors and windows. This removes hiding places and lets neighbors see your home. Thorny plants such as roses or barberry under ground-floor windows discourage anyone from standing there. Keep fences low or see-through in front so the entry is visible from the street. Store ladders, tools, and patio furniture that could be used to climb or break in.

steps.title: Show that someone cares for the place
steps.body: Well-kept homes signal that people are watching. Mow the lawn, pick up trash, fix broken windows and blinds quickly, and paint over graffiti right away. Keep house numbers large, lighted, and visible from the street so police, fire, and EMS can find you fast. When away, stop mail and deliveries or have a neighbor collect them, and keep the garage door closed. Break down boxes from expensive purchases before putting them out, so you do not advertise new electronics or generators.

steps.title: Get a free review and keep it up
steps.body: Many police departments offer free CPTED or home security reviews; call your non-emergency line and ask. Walk your property every season, after storms, and after the time change to check lights, locks, and plant growth. Write a short list of what to fix and do one item each weekend. Teach everyone in the house to lock up every time, including during the day. The best hardware does nothing if a door is left unlocked.

warnings: Never block fire escape routes. Every sleeping room needs a way out that opens fast from inside.
Double-cylinder deadbolts and window bars can trap people in a fire. Follow local code and use quick-release bars.
Do not install devices meant to injure intruders. They are illegal and dangerous to family and responders.
If you come home and a door or window is forced, do not go in. Leave and call 911 from a safe place.
proTips: Swapping strike-plate screws for 3-inch screws costs a few dollars and is one of the best upgrades you can make.
Solar motion lights are a cheap way to keep lighting during long outages.
Photograph or record serial numbers for valuables - it helps police and insurance.
Ask a neighbor to park in your driveway when you are away.
source: Seattle PD Crime Prevention / Liberty MO and Menlo Park PD CPTED
whenNotTo: Do not board up or bar windows in a way that traps your family during a fire.
Renters: check your lease and ask the landlord before changing locks or frames.

quickGlance.situation: You want to make your home less attractive to burglars and safer during long emergencies.
immediate: Replace strike-plate screws with 3-4 inch screws into the stud
Bar sliding doors and lock every window
Light all entrances and trim shrubs to about 2 ft
then: Keep bedroom fire exits clear and quick to open
Ask your police department for a free home security review

title: OPSEC: Keeping Your Supplies and Plans Private
summary: Keep quiet about what you have and where you will be, so your home and family are not singled out when supplies run short. Privacy is not secrecy from everyone - it is choosing who knows what.

steps.title: Decide what needs to stay private
steps.body: Operations security, or OPSEC, means protecting small details that add up to a target. For a family, the sensitive details are: how much food, water, fuel, and cash you have, whether you own a generator, when the house is empty, travel plans, where you will evacuate, and which family members are home alone. None of this is shameful. It just does not need to be public. Make a short list with your household so everyone, including teens, knows what not to share.

steps.title: Lock down social media
steps.body: The FBI warns that announcing where you are - and where you are not - helps criminals. Set accounts to the most private settings, limit followers to people you know in person, and turn off automatic location tags. Do not post flight details, hotel names, or evacuation routes. Wait until you are home to share trip photos. Do not post photos of your pantry, gear room, gun safe, generator, or cash, and check the background of pictures for house numbers, mail, or car plates. Scammers also use travel posts to target relatives.

steps.title: Watch what your trash and deliveries say
steps.body: A generator box or a stack of bulk-food cases at the curb tells the whole street what you just bought. Break boxes down and put them inside your recycling bin, or wait until pickup day. Bring deliveries inside quickly, and use a pickup location for large orders if you prefer. Keep the garage door closed so shelves of supplies are not on display. Store supplies in plain bins rather than labeled boxes in areas visitors might see.

steps.title: Talk on a need-to-know basis
steps.body: Share your full plans only with the people who need them: household members, your out-of-area contact, and the friends or relatives you plan to stay with. Coworkers, casual acquaintances, and strangers in line do not need to know you have a month of food. Teach children a simple line, such as 'We're doing okay, thanks,' and explain that it is a family rule, not a lie. If you are asked directly by someone you do not know well, a friendly, vague answer is fine.

steps.title: Keep a low profile during an outage
steps.body: When most of the street is dark and quiet, a brightly lit house with a loud generator stands out. Use curtains or blinds at night, keep lights to the rooms you are using, and run the generator only when needed. Follow generator safety without exception: outdoors only, at least 20 feet (6 m) from doors and windows, never in a garage. Chain it to something solid if theft is a concern. Cook smells and music carry, so keep them modest at night. A low profile is about not drawing attention, not about hiding from help.

steps.title: Share wisely with neighbors
steps.body: Complete secrecy can backfire, because neighbors are your best early warning and support. You can build strong ties without listing your inventory. Offer help with skills and time, check on older neighbors, and give modest amounts of food or water when someone is in need. Many families keep a small 'sharing' supply set aside so they can help without revealing everything. Be honest with police, fire, and emergency officials when they ask about needs or hazards such as stored fuel, since that keeps responders safe.

warnings: Never lie to police, fire, or emergency officials. Tell them about hazards like stored fuel, propane, or oxygen tanks.
Never run a generator indoors or in a garage to keep it hidden. Carbon monoxide can kill in minutes.
Do not let privacy stop you from asking for help when you are hurt or in danger.
proTips: Post trip photos after you get home - the FBI recommends it.
Keep a small, separate 'sharing' box of water and snacks so you can help neighbors without opening your main supply.
Turn off location services for camera apps so photos do not carry GPS data.
Do a quarterly check of your public social media profile from a logged-out browser to see what strangers see.
source: FBI / U.S. Air Force travel safety guidance

sources.title: FBI Tech Tuesday: Building a Digital Defense Against the Dangers of Using Social Media While Traveling
sources.publisher: Federal Bureau of Investigation, Portland Field Office

sources.title: Holiday a good time to travel, but stay smart
sources.publisher: U.S. Air Force, 501st Combat Support Wing

whenNotTo: Do not keep needs secret from emergency responders or medical staff.
Do not hide a family member's medical needs from shelter staff - they need to know to help.

quickGlance.situation: Supplies may run short around you and you do not want your home singled out.
immediate: Stop posting supplies, travel, and evacuation plans online
Break down boxes and keep the garage closed
Use curtains at night and run generators only outdoors, 20+ ft from the house
then: Share plans only with people who need them
Help neighbors from a small separate 'sharing' supply

title: The Gray Man: Blending In and Avoiding Attention in a Crisis
summary: Look, dress, and act like an ordinary, calm person so you are less likely to be picked out as a target when things are tense. The goal is simply to not stand out - never to deceive police or avoid help.

steps.title: Know what the gray man idea really is
steps.body: 'Gray man' is a nickname for a person nobody remembers: dressed like everyone else, carrying an ordinary bag, calm, and going about normal business. People looking for an easy target tend to notice whoever stands out - the flashy, the lost, the distracted, or the person with obviously valuable gear. Blending in will not make you invisible, but it lowers the odds that you are the one singled out. It works with good awareness (sec-001), not instead of it.

steps.title: Dress like the people around you
steps.body: Wear plain, practical clothes in common colors that fit the weather and the place. Skip camouflage, tactical-looking vests, military patches, and gear covered in brand logos for outdoor or survival companies; they suggest you have valuable equipment. Avoid expensive jewelry and watches. Good, broken-in walking shoes matter more than looks. Military travel guidance gives the same advice for service members abroad: blend in with the crowd and stay low key.

steps.title: Carry gear and money out of sight
steps.body: Use an ordinary backpack, tote, or grocery bag instead of a large tactical pack. Keep cash in more than one place and carry only what you need for the day; never flash a thick wallet in a line. Keep your ID and important papers on your body, not in a bag you might set down. Keep a phone out only while using it. If you are carrying water or supplies home after a distribution, cover them and go straight home rather than stopping in busy places.

steps.title: Move with calm purpose
steps.body: People who look lost, rushed, or frightened draw attention. Check your map before you leave or step into a shop to look at it, then walk at a normal pace with your head up as if you know where you are going. Keep your voice at a normal level and be polite in lines. Avoid arguing about politics, the disaster, or who deserves aid. If someone tries to start a conflict, do not take the bait - a quiet 'Sorry, I'm just getting water' and moving on is a strong choice.

steps.title: Avoid hot spots and bad timing
steps.body: Stay away from protests, rallies, and crowds that are getting angry, even if you agree with them; they can turn quickly. Do errands in daylight, in small groups, and at less busy times. Choose well-lit, populated routes over shortcuts. Tell someone where you are going and when you expect to be back. If an area feels wrong, leave and come back another time or use a different site.

steps.title: Know when to stand out
steps.body: Blending in is for avoiding trouble, not for avoiding help. Stand out on purpose when you need rescue (bright colors, signals, waving down responders), when you need medical care, and when you are giving information to police. Never hide from or mislead police, National Guard, or emergency workers; follow their instructions and identify yourself when asked. If a family member is lost, make yourself visible at the agreed meeting place.

warnings: Do not use 'gray man' ideas to dodge police, checkpoints, or curfews. That can be illegal and dangerous.
Blending in is not a reason to skip a reflective vest or flashlight when walking near roads at night.
If you are being followed, go into an open business or toward police and call 911 - do not try to lose them on your own in quiet areas.
proTips: Put a plain cover or a cheap tote bag over a technical backpack when walking in town.
Keep a small amount of 'give-up' cash separate from your main money.
Copy what calm locals do in a new place - where they wait, how they dress, which routes they take.
Practice walking a new route with a paper map before you need it so you do not look lost later.
source: U.S. Air Force travel safety / FBI

sources.title: Holiday a good time to travel, but stay smart
sources.publisher: U.S. Air Force, 501st Combat Support Wing

sources.title: FBI Tech Tuesday: Building a Digital Defense Against the Dangers of Using Social Media While Traveling

sources.title: Survival, Evasion, and Recovery: Multiservice Procedures (FM 21-76-1, 1999)
