whenNotTo: When you need rescue or medical help - make yourself as visible as possible.
When police or officials ask who you are - identify yourself and follow instructions.

quickGlance.situation: You must go out during a tense crisis - for water, supplies, or travel - and want to avoid being singled out.
immediate: Dress plainly; skip tactical gear and flashy items
Carry supplies in an ordinary bag and keep cash hidden
Walk calmly with purpose and avoid crowds and protests
then: Do errands in daylight in small groups and tell someone your plan
Stand out on purpose when you need help

title: Scams and Fraud After Disasters
summary: Scammers move in right after disasters, posing as FEMA staff, utility workers, contractors, and charities. Learn the red flags and how to verify anyone before you pay or share personal information.

steps.title: Know the main scams
steps.body: After storms, floods, and fires, the most common scams are: fake government workers who ask for money or bank details to 'speed up' aid; utility imposters who say your service will be cut off unless you pay now; door-to-door contractors who take a deposit and disappear or do poor work; fake charities that collect donations for victims; and phishing texts and emails with links to fake aid sites. They all share three signs: pressure to act right now, a request for payment or personal information, and an unusual payment method.

steps.title: Verify anyone who says they are from FEMA
steps.body: FEMA does not charge for inspections, help applying, or any assistance, and real disaster workers never ask for or accept money. FEMA staff and contractors carry a laminated photo ID badge - ask to see it. A shirt or jacket with a FEMA logo is not proof. Real inspectors contact you to set an appointment and may call from unfamiliar area codes, but they already have your application number. If you are unsure, do not share anything; call the FEMA Helpline at 800-621-3362 to confirm the call or visit. Apply only at DisasterAssistance.gov, the FEMA app, or the Helpline.

steps.title: Check out contractors before you sign
steps.body: The FTC advises hiring only licensed and insured contractors. Check the license with your state or county licensing office, ask for proof of insurance, and get several written estimates. Be wary of anyone who knocks on your door, says they have leftover materials, or offers a deal only if you decide today. Get a written contract that lists the work, price, timeline, and who pulls permits. Never sign over your insurance check or let a contractor deal with your insurer on your behalf without reading every page.

steps.title: Pay the safe way
steps.body: Do not pay in cash for repairs or debris removal. A credit card gives you more protection if the work is not done. Scammers ask for gift cards, wire transfers, payment apps, or cryptocurrency because the money is almost impossible to get back. Pay a reasonable deposit only if required by your state's rules, and pay the balance only after the work is finished and you are satisfied. Keep copies of every contract, receipt, and text message.

steps.title: Handle utility and phone calls carefully
steps.body: If someone calls or comes to the door saying they are from the power, water, or gas company and you must pay now, do not pay. Ask for identification and verify by calling the number on your bill or the utility's official website, not a number they give you. Treat texts and emails about disaster aid, refunds, or account problems the same way: do not click links. Go directly to the official site by typing the address yourself.

steps.title: Give to charities you can verify
steps.body: Give to well-known relief groups you already trust, and go to their website directly rather than through a link in a text, email, or social media post. Be cautious of new groups with names that sound like famous charities, crowdfunding pages you cannot confirm, and anyone who pushes you to give immediately or only accepts cash, gift cards, or wire transfers. Your state attorney general or charity regulator can tell you whether an organization is registered.

steps.title: Report scams and protect your identity
steps.body: Report disaster fraud to the FEMA Disaster Fraud Hotline at 866-720-5721 (24/7) or disaster@leo.gov, and to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. Report it to local police as well, especially if someone came to your home. If you gave out your Social Security number or bank details, act fast: call your bank, place a fraud alert or credit freeze, and follow the steps in sec-015. Warn neighbors - scammers often work an entire street.

warnings: FEMA never charges fees and real disaster workers never accept money. Anyone asking for payment is a scammer.
Never pay with gift cards, wire transfers, or cryptocurrency for disaster help or repairs.
Do not let anyone pressure you into signing a contract on the spot, especially while you are in shock.
Older adults are targeted often. Check in on elderly relatives and neighbors after a disaster.
proTips: Write your FEMA application number on a card. Real FEMA contacts can refer to it; scammers usually cannot.
Save FEMA's Helpline (800-621-3362) and the fraud hotline (866-720-5721) in your phone and on paper before storm season.
Take photos of a contractor's license, truck plate, and ID before they start work.
The FTC has free disaster-scam handouts at ftc.gov/WeatherEmergencies you can share with neighbors.

sources.title: Beware of Fraud and Scams (fact sheet)
Four ways to avoid scams after a weather-related disaster
Plan to avoid scams this National Preparedness Month

whenNotTo: Do not refuse a real, scheduled FEMA inspection - verify it through the Helpline instead.
Do not delay emergency repairs that prevent more damage, such as tarping a roof; just use a verified contractor and keep receipts.

quickGlance.situation: After a disaster, someone contacts you offering aid, repairs, or a chance to donate.
immediate: Do not pay or share personal info on the spot
Ask for a photo ID badge; call FEMA at 800-621-3362 to verify
Never pay cash, gift cards, wires, or crypto
then: Hire licensed, insured contractors with a written contract; pay in full only when done
Report fraud: 866-720-5721 or ReportFraud.ftc.gov

title: De-escalation: Calming Tense Situations and Dealing With Strangers
summary: Use calm words, body language, and distance to cool down an angry person or a tense exchange with strangers - and know when to stop talking and leave. Based on CISA's Recognize, Assess, De-escalate, Report approach.

steps.title: Recognize the warning signs
steps.body: Tension usually builds in steps. Watch for a voice getting louder or faster, pacing, clenched fists, a red face, staring, swearing, getting closer and closer, and statements like 'You'll be sorry.' CISA calls this recognizing changes from a person's normal behavior. Stress after a disaster - lost homes, no sleep, hunger, worry about family - makes almost everyone shorter-tempered. Spotting rising tension early gives you the best chance to calm it or step away before it turns physical.

steps.title: Assess: is it safe to stay?
steps.body: Before you try to calm anyone, ask yourself: Is anyone threatening violence or showing a weapon? Is the person drunk or high? Am I trapped, or do I have a clear way out? Are children or others at risk? If violence looks likely or has started, do not try to talk it down - move away to safety and call 911. CISA's guidance is clear that your safety comes first and that you should know your limits and get help. De-escalation is a tool for tense moments, not for active danger.

steps.title: Set up your space and body language
steps.body: Keep at least two arm's lengths of distance and stand at a slight angle rather than squarely facing the person. Keep your hands down, open, and visible. Move slowly and do not point, touch, or block their way out. Keep your own exit open behind or beside you. Use a neutral, attentive face. If possible, move the conversation somewhere quieter, away from an audience, but never into an isolated spot. Small changes like sitting down or stepping back can lower the temperature without a word.

steps.title: Use your voice to lower the heat
steps.body: Speak calmly, a little slower and quieter than normal; people often match your tone. Use short, simple sentences. Use their name if you know it. Listen more than you talk, and show you heard them: 'You've been waiting since this morning and you're worried about your kids. That's rough.' Acknowledging feelings is not agreeing. Avoid commands, sarcasm, arguing facts, and phrases like 'calm down,' which usually backfire. Do not make promises you cannot keep.

steps.title: Look for what they actually need
steps.body: Anger after a disaster is often about a real need: water, medicine, news of family, fairness, or respect. Ask open questions: 'What do you need most right now?' Then offer realistic choices: 'I can't let you in, but I can point you to the shelter on Main Street, and I can give you a bottle of water.' Giving a person two acceptable options helps them feel in control. When dealing with strangers at your home, talk through a closed door or window, keep the door locked, and direct them to official aid sites rather than inviting them inside.

steps.title: Know when to disengage
steps.body: If the person keeps escalating, threatens you, reaches for something, or will not let you leave, stop talking and go. Say something simple and non-threatening, like 'I'm going to go now,' and leave toward people and lights. At home, close and lock the door, move to an inner room, and call 911. You do not need to win the argument or have the last word. Getting away is a success.

steps.title: Report what happened
steps.body: After the situation ends, tell someone who can act on it: shelter staff, site security, or police. Call 911 right away if there was a threat of violence. Share facts only - what the person said and did, when, where, and what they looked like - without guesses about why. CISA notes that reports should be based on behavior, not on someone's race, religion, gender, age, or disability. Your report may prevent the next person from being hurt.

warnings: Never try to talk down someone who has a weapon or is already attacking. Leave and call 911.
Do not touch, corner, or block an agitated person; it often triggers violence.
Do not open your door or let strangers inside during a crisis. Talk through the door and point them to official aid.
Alcohol and drugs make people unpredictable. Give extra distance and leave sooner.
proTips: Practice a few calm phrases ahead of time so they come out naturally under stress.
Lower your volume when they raise theirs; it often pulls their volume down too.
Work in pairs at aid tables or gates, so one person can talk while the other watches and gets help.
If you are wrong about something, saying 'You're right, I'm sorry' can end a conflict instantly.
source: CISA De-escalation Series and Action Guide
whenNotTo: Someone has a weapon, is attacking, or is threatening violence right now - leave and call 911.
You are trapped alone with the person - focus on getting out, not on talking.

quickGlance.situation: Someone is getting angry or a stranger is pressing you for help or entry during a crisis.
immediate: Check for danger - weapon or threats means leave and call 911
Keep two arm's lengths, hands open and visible, exit clear
Speak slowly and quietly; listen and acknowledge feelings
then: Offer realistic options and point to official aid
If it keeps escalating, disengage, lock up, and report

title: Active Threat: Run, Hide, Fight
summary: The federal Run, Hide, Fight guidance for surviving an active shooter or other attacker: get out if you can, hide well if you cannot, and act against the attacker only as a last resort when your life is at risk.

steps.title: Prepare before it happens
steps.body: Attacks often end within minutes, before police can arrive, so your first choices matter. Wherever you spend time - work, school, church, stores - learn at least two exits and notice rooms with doors that lock. Pay attention to warning signs and report concerning behavior or threats to police, staff, or a supervisor. Talk with your family about what they would do. Knowing the plan ahead of time helps you break through the freeze reaction that slows most people.

steps.title: RUN - get out if there is a safe path
steps.body: If you hear gunfire or see an attack and there is a way out, leave immediately. Leave your belongings behind. Urge others to come, but do not wait if they will not. Help others escape if you can do so safely. Once you are out, keep going and keep others from walking into the area. When you see police, keep your hands empty and visible. Running away is the best option whenever it is possible - it puts distance between you and the danger.

steps.title: HIDE - if you cannot get out
steps.body: If escape is not possible, hide where the attacker is unlikely to find you, ideally out of sight and behind something solid. Choose a room with a door that locks and lock it. Block the door with heavy furniture. Turn off lights, silence your phone completely including vibration, and stay quiet. Stay away from the door and crouch behind sturdy objects. Do not trap yourself with no options if you can avoid it. Stay hidden until police tell you it is safe.

steps.title: Call or text 911 when it is safe
steps.body: When you can do so without giving away your position, call 911 and tell the dispatcher there is an active attacker. Give your location, the number of attackers, what they look like, and what weapons you saw if you know. If you cannot speak, leave the line open so the dispatcher can listen, or text 911 if your area supports it. Do not assume someone else has already called.

steps.title: FIGHT - only as a last resort
steps.body: If your life is in immediate danger and you cannot run or hide, federal guidance says to act against the attacker with as much force as you can. This is a desperate measure, not a plan. Commit fully if you must: throw things, yell, use any object at hand, and act together with others if possible. The aim is to disrupt the attack long enough to escape or survive. If the attacker is stopped, get away and tell police exactly what happened and where any weapons are.

steps.title: When police arrive
steps.body: The first officers are there to stop the threat. They may not stop to help injured people right away, and they do not know who the attacker is. Stay calm and follow every command. Drop anything in your hands and keep your hands raised and open. Do not point, yell, grab, or run toward officers. Leave the way they direct you, and stay at the area they set up until you have been questioned, because your information may help.

steps.title: Care for the injured and yourself
steps.body: Once you are safe, help injured people if you can. Firm pressure on heavy bleeding can save a life while EMS is on the way; a Stop the Bleed class teaches this in about an hour. Check yourself too - adrenaline can hide injuries. In the days after, it is normal to feel shaky, numb, or unable to sleep. Talk to people you trust, and contact a doctor, counselor, or the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline if distress does not ease.

warnings: Never go toward gunfire to see what is happening.
Keep your hands empty and visible when police arrive. Do not run at them or grab them.
Do not leave a safe hiding place until police say it is safe - attackers sometimes pretend to be help.
Fighting is only for when your life is in immediate danger and you cannot escape or hide.
proTips: Some agencies now say 'active assailant' or 'active threat' because attacks may use vehicles, knives, or other weapons. The same Run, Hide, Fight steps apply.
Take a free Stop the Bleed class and keep a tourniquet in your car or bag.
At events, sit near an exit and note where the side doors are.
Teach children a simple version: get out, hide and stay quiet, wait for police.
source: DHS / CISA Run, Hide, Fight via Defense Logistics Agency

sources.title: What to do in an active shooter event

whenNotTo: Do not run if the only path leads toward the attacker - hide instead.
Do not fight if you can still safely run or hide.

quickGlance.situation: Someone is attacking people nearby with a gun or other weapon.
immediate: RUN if there is a safe way out - leave belongings
HIDE if you cannot get out - lock, block, lights off, phone silent
Call or text 911 when safe
then: FIGHT only as a last resort when your life is in immediate danger
When police arrive, show empty hands and follow commands

title: Firearm Safety and Safe Storage
summary: If there is a firearm in your home or vehicle, these universal safety rules and storage practices help prevent accidents, theft, and tragedies involving children or people in crisis. Always follow your federal, state, and local laws.

steps.title: Learn the universal safety rules
steps.body: Every safety course teaches the same core rules. Treat every firearm as if it is loaded, even if you think it is not. Always keep the muzzle pointed in a safe direction. Never point a firearm at any person or anything you are not willing to destroy. Keep your finger off the trigger until you are ready to fire. Know what is beyond your target. These rules apply equally to BB, pellet, airsoft, and paintball guns, which can cause serious injuries, especially to eyes.

steps.title: Store firearms locked and unloaded
steps.body: When a firearm is not under your direct control, store it unloaded and locked in a gun safe, biometric safe, or hardened lockbox. Store ammunition separately and locked as well. A cable lock or trigger lock adds another layer and is often given free by local police or safety programs. Never leave a firearm unattended once it is out, even for a minute. Hiding a gun in a closet, drawer, or under a mattress is not safe storage - children and visitors find hidden guns.

steps.title: Protect children
steps.body: Keep keys and combinations where children cannot get them; do not use birthdays or other easy-to-guess codes. Teach children of all ages a simple rule: if you see a gun, stop, do not touch, leave the area, and tell an adult. Practice it calmly. Before your child visits another home, it is reasonable to ask whether there are firearms and how they are stored. If children visit your home, let their parents know you store firearms safely. Many states have child access prevention laws that hold adults responsible if a child gets an unsecured gun.

steps.title: Plan for crisis and disaster
steps.body: Firearms in a home where someone is in a mental health crisis greatly raise the risk of suicide. If a household member is struggling, consider temporary storage outside the home with a trusted person, a gun shop, or police where local law allows; call or text 988 for support. In a disaster, your storage plan still applies: if you evacuate, either take the firearm in a locked case following transport laws or keep it in a bolted safe. Red Cross and most public shelters do not allow weapons, so plan ahead for where it will be stored.

steps.title: Secure firearms in vehicles and on the move
steps.body: Vehicles are a major source of stolen guns. Never leave a firearm in a parked car unless it is in a locked container that is secured to the vehicle, and only where legal. Keep it out of sight. Transport unloaded in a locked case when the law requires, and look up the rules for every state and city you will pass through, since they differ widely. Federal buildings, schools, airports, and many shelters prohibit firearms.

steps.title: Know and follow the law
steps.body: Laws on buying, owning, carrying, storing, and transporting firearms vary by state, county, and city, and they change. Learn the rules where you live and where you travel. Emergency declarations can also bring temporary rules, so check official announcements. Using force in self-defense is governed by strict laws; a firearm is never a tool for protecting property alone or for settling a dispute. If you have questions, ask your local police department or a qualified attorney.

steps.title: Train, keep records, and dispose of guns properly
steps.body: Take a certified firearm safety course covering safe handling, cleaning, and storage. Keep a record of each firearm's make, model, and serial number in a secure place separate from the gun, so you can report it if stolen. Store ammunition in proper containers away from heat and moisture. To get rid of an unwanted firearm or old ammunition, contact your local police department for safe, legal disposal - do not throw them in the trash.

warnings: Unsecured firearms are a leading cause of preventable child deaths and of suicides. Lock them up every time.
Never handle a firearm while using alcohol, drugs, or medicines that cause drowsiness.
Most public shelters prohibit weapons. Plan ahead for safe storage if you evacuate.
Laws vary widely by place and change. Always follow your federal, state, and local laws.
proTips: Many police departments and safety programs give out free cable locks - ask at your local station.
Use a quick-access biometric or keypad lockbox if you want secure storage that is still fast for you to open.
Write the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline number in your family plan. Temporary off-site storage during a crisis saves lives.
Store your firearm serial number list with your important documents (see sec-015).
source: Indiana Dept. of Education firearm storage best practices

sources.title: Best Practices in Safe Possession and Storage of Firearms
Welcome to Your Red Cross Shelter

whenNotTo: This guide is not training in shooting or defensive use. Take a certified course for hands-on instruction.
If anyone in the home is in crisis, focus on getting the firearm out of the home temporarily and getting support.

quickGlance.situation: There is a firearm in your home or vehicle, especially with children or visitors around or during a disaster.
immediate: Treat every firearm as loaded and keep the muzzle pointed safely
Store unloaded and locked; lock ammunition separately
Teach kids: stop, don't touch, leave, tell an adult
then: Use temporary off-site storage if someone is in crisis; call or text 988
Check local laws for transport and shelters before you evacuate

title: Neighborhood Watch and Setting Up a Night Watch Rotation
summary: Organize neighbors to watch out for each other and, during long outages, set up a safe night watch rotation built around one rule: observe and report, never confront.

steps.title: Start with neighbors who can see each other
steps.body: A neighborhood watch begins with a handful of households that can see each other's homes. Knock on doors, explain the goal - looking out for each other and reporting problems to police - and set a meeting time. The National Neighborhood Watch Institute, working with the National Sheriffs' Association, suggests reaching out about four weeks before the first meeting and inviting a local law enforcement officer at least two weeks ahead. Keep the first meeting to about 90 minutes and focused on getting started, not on every complaint.

steps.title: Partner with law enforcement and pick leaders
steps.body: Choose a block captain or watch coordinator to be the link with your police or sheriff's office. Ask the officer what kinds of activity to report, when to call 911 versus the non-emergency line, and what information helps them most. A watch is not a vigilante group and members do not take personal risks to stop crime. Members watch from their own homes and report. That rule protects your neighbors legally and physically.

steps.title: Build your contact tools
steps.body: Have each household fill out a simple data sheet: names, phone numbers, vehicles, who has medical needs or mobility limits, and who has useful skills such as nursing or electrical work. Use it to make a phone tree, a group text, and a hand-drawn block map. Print copies, because phones and internet may fail. For outages, agree on a backup: FRS/GMRS handheld radios on an agreed channel, a whistle signal, or a runner system. Keep the sheet private to members.

steps.title: Decide when a night watch is needed
steps.body: In normal times, a regular watch plus porch lights is enough. During a long power outage or after a major disaster, when streetlights are out and response times are long, some neighborhoods set up a night watch. The purpose is early warning: spotting fires, gas leaks, medical emergencies, flooding, and suspicious activity, and getting help quickly. It is not about patrolling or guarding streets. Check with local police first, and follow any curfew.

steps.title: Set up a safe rotation
steps.body: Use two-person shifts so no one watches alone and someone can always call for help. Keep shifts short, about 2 to 3 hours, so people stay alert, and rotate so the same people do not always get the worst hours. Watchers stay at a home with a good view - a porch, window, or yard - and do not wander the street. Each pair needs a charged phone or radio, a flashlight, a reflective vest, a notepad, and the contact list. The next pair should be fully awake before the handoff.

steps.title: Observe, write it down, and report
steps.body: When something seems wrong, watchers stay where they are, observe from a distance, and call 911 for emergencies or the non-emergency line for concerns. Note the time, what happened, descriptions of people by clothing and height, vehicles and plates, and direction of travel. Keep a simple log so the next shift knows what happened. Never follow, confront, block, or try to detain anyone. Warn neighbors by phone tree or radio if needed, then let trained responders handle it.

steps.title: Look after the people in the watch
steps.body: Sleep is the hardest part of a long watch. Make sure every adult gets at least one long sleep block, and excuse people with health problems, young children, or early work. Check on older neighbors and anyone living alone during each shift. Keep meetings short and friendly and share news from officials. A watch that also checks on people and shares resources holds a neighborhood together through a long emergency.

warnings: Watch members observe and report only. Never follow, confront, or try to detain anyone.
Do not carry weapons on watch duty. Armed patrols escalate situations and create serious legal risk.
Never watch alone at night - work in pairs and keep a phone or radio at hand.
Follow curfews and police instructions; a night watch stays on members' own property.
proTips: Reflective vests and porch lights make watchers easy for police to recognize as neighbors.
Pick one radio channel for the block and test it monthly, so it works when phones fail.
Put the watch log in a shared notebook kept at one house so every shift can read it.
Invite your local officer back once a year for a refresher.
source: National Neighborhood Watch Institute / National Sheriffs' Association

sources.title: Start a Neighborhood Watch
sources.publisher: National Neighborhood Watch Institute / National Sheriffs' Association

whenNotTo: Do not start a night watch during a curfew without checking with police.
Do not use a watch to target people based on race, appearance, or being new to the area.

quickGlance.situation: Your street wants to look out for each other, especially during a long outage when police response is slow.
immediate: Gather neighbors who can see each other's homes and invite a local officer
Build a contact list, phone tree, and block map on paper
Set the rule: observe and report, never confront
then: For long outages, run 2-person, 2-3 hour shifts from members' own porches
Log what you see and call 911 for emergencies

title: Checkpoints, Curfews, and Dealing With Police or National Guard in Emergencies
summary: Know what to carry, how to behave, and what your basic rights are when you meet police, deputies, or National Guard at checkpoints and under curfews after a disaster - so the encounter stays calm, safe, and short.

steps.title: Understand why checkpoints and curfews happen
steps.body: After a disaster, officials may close roads, set up checkpoints, and order curfews to keep people out of dangerous areas, protect empty homes from looting, and keep routes clear for crews. Re-entry often happens in phases: first public safety and utility crews, then residents once areas are assessed. National Guard members may staff checkpoints alongside local police, usually under the governor's authority. Treat their instructions the same way you would treat a police officer's. Follow local news, NOAA Weather Radio, and official emergency management social media for current rules.

steps.title: Carry the right documents
steps.body: Keep a government-issued photo ID that shows your home address. If your ID shows an old address, carry proof of residence such as a utility bill, lease, deed, or property tax bill. Some counties issue re-entry passes or tags ahead of hurricane or fire season - sign up if yours does. Business owners may need a business license or letter; essential workers may need a letter on company letterhead. Keep copies in your go bag and photos on your phone (see sec-015).

steps.title: Approach a checkpoint calmly
steps.body: Slow down early and follow signs and hand signals. Turn off music, lower your window, and at night turn on your interior light. Keep both hands on the steering wheel where officers can see them. Tell the officer before you reach for anything: 'My ID is in my wallet in my back pocket - may I get it?' Answer basic questions about where you are going. Keep passengers calm and hands visible too. If you are turned away, accept it and leave by the route they direct - arguing will not change the decision, and the supervisor at each checkpoint decides who can enter.

steps.title: Follow curfews and know exemptions
steps.body: Curfews limit when people can be outside, and they vary by place. Many allow exceptions for going to or from work, getting food or medical care, caring for a family member, and emergencies, but check the exact order where you are. If you must be out during curfew, carry proof of the reason, such as a work badge or letter. If stopped, stay polite and explain briefly. A curfew does not remove your constitutional rights, but officers do have broad power during an emergency to warn, cite, or arrest.

steps.title: Know your basic rights - and stay calm
steps.body: In general, you can decline to answer questions beyond identifying yourself where required, and you can say, 'I wish to remain silent.' You can say you do not consent to a search, but do not physically resist if officers search anyway. Ask 'Am I free to go?' if you are unsure. Never run, argue, resist, or give false information or documents. Drivers must show license, registration, and insurance when asked. Rules vary by state, so learn yours. Challenges to a stop are made later through complaints or the courts, not on the roadside.

steps.title: If a checkpoint seems unofficial
steps.body: Real checkpoints usually have marked vehicles, uniforms, lights, and signs. If something seems wrong - no markings, people in mixed clothing, demands for money or goods - stay in your locked vehicle, keep calm, and do not argue. If you can safely turn around or avoid it, do so, then call 911 and report its location. If you are already stopped, comply with demands for property rather than risk injury; property can be replaced. Report it to police as soon as you are safe.

steps.title: Write it down afterward
steps.body: After any encounter that concerned you, write down what happened while it is fresh: time, place, agency, officer names, badge and vehicle numbers, and any witnesses. If you were hurt, get medical care first and photograph injuries. You can file a complaint with the agency or a civilian review board, and civil rights groups can advise you. If the encounter went well, thank them - checkpoint crews often work long shifts in hard conditions.

warnings: Never drive around barricades or through a checkpoint. Roads are often closed for real hazards like downed lines or washed-out bridges.
Do not run, argue, or physically resist officers, even if you think a stop is unfair. Use complaints and the courts later.
Never give false ID or false information to officers.
Rules vary by state and change during emergencies. This is general information, not legal advice.
proTips: Ask your county emergency management office now whether they use re-entry passes, and keep yours in the car.
Keep a utility bill copy in your go bag if your license shows an old address.
Keep your registration and insurance card in one easy-to-reach envelope so you are not digging around.
Expect long waits at re-entry checkpoints - bring water, snacks, and a full tank.
source: Horry County SC Emergency Management / ACLU know-your-rights guidance

sources.title: Hurricane Re-Entry Brochure
sources.publisher: Horry County Emergency Management, South Carolina

sources.title: Know Your Rights: Law Enforcement Encounters
What to know if you're stopped by law enforcement after curfew

whenNotTo: This is not legal advice. For a specific legal problem, talk to a qualified attorney.
In a medical emergency during curfew, call 911 rather than driving through checkpoints yourself if possible.

quickGlance.situation: You are approaching a checkpoint, are out during a curfew, or are stopped by police or National Guard after a disaster.
immediate: Slow down, interior light on at night, hands on the wheel
Have photo ID with your address and proof of residence ready
Say what you are reaching for before you move; stay calm and polite
then: If turned away, leave by the route directed
Write down details afterward; use complaints, not arguments, for problems

title: Personal Safety in Shelters, Crowds, and Evacuation Centers
summary: Stay safe and protect your belongings in public shelters, evacuation centers, and crowded aid sites. Know the rules, keep children close, use the buddy system, and bring problems to staff.

steps.title: Know the shelter rules before you arrive
steps.body: Red Cross shelters do not allow alcohol, illegal drugs, or weapons of any kind, including concealed weapons, inside or on the grounds. Smoking is allowed only outside in designated spots. Abusive behavior, stealing, and property damage are not tolerated. Everyone is screened and registered, and you sign in and out each time you leave or return. These rules protect you. If you carry a firearm legally, plan before you arrive where it will be stored safely and lawfully, because you will not be able to bring it in (see sec-011).

steps.title: Register honestly and share your needs
steps.body: Fill out the family registration form and tell the worker about medical needs, disabilities, medications that need a fridge, service animals, and anything that makes you feel unsafe. Shelter staff can sometimes place families together, find a quieter area, or connect you with nurses and mental health workers. If you are fleeing domestic violence or someone in the shelter worries you, tell staff privately. You can leave unknown parts of the form blank.

steps.title: Protect your valuables
steps.body: Bring as few valuables as possible. Your belongings must fit under your cot, and the Red Cross cannot take responsibility for them. Lock valuables in your car out of sight if you have one; otherwise keep them on your body. Wear a small cross-body bag or money belt for ID, phone, cash, and medicines. Label chargers, bags, and medical equipment with your name. Keep medicines with you instead of in a bag on the floor. Do not show cash or talk about what you have.

steps.title: Keep children close and use the buddy system
steps.body: Parents are responsible for supervising their children at all times; children should never be left alone in the shelter. Use the buddy system for bathrooms, showers, and walks outside, especially at night - adults too. Teach children who the shelter workers are (usually vests or badges) and to go to them if they are scared or lost. Give each child a card with your name, cot location, and phone number. Agree on a meeting spot inside the shelter, such as the registration desk.

steps.title: Stay alert in crowds and lines
steps.body: At aid lines, fuel stations, and busy shelters, keep to the edge of the crowd, know where the exits are, and keep your bag in front of you. Be patient and polite - tempers are short when people are tired and scared. If a crowd starts pushing or surging, do not fight against it. Move diagonally toward the edges, keep your arms up in front of your chest to protect your breathing, and stay on your feet. If you fall, get up fast. Leave lines that feel unsafe and come back later.

steps.title: Bring problems to staff early
steps.body: If someone is threatening, harassing, stealing, or making you uneasy, do not handle it yourself. Tell a shelter worker or security officer right away, and call 911 if anyone is in immediate danger. Report facts: who, what, when, and where. Shelter staff can move cots, involve police, or remove people who break the rules. Use calm de-escalation if you are drawn into a tense moment, and step away instead of arguing (see sec-009).

steps.title: Stay connected and leave safely
steps.body: Keep your out-of-area contact updated. When you leave the shelter, register at the Red Cross Safe and Well site so loved ones can find you, and sign out with staff. Only go home when officials say your area is safe. Watch for scammers who target people leaving shelters with offers of repairs, rentals, or quick aid money (see sec-008).

warnings: Never leave children unattended in a shelter.
Weapons, alcohol, and drugs are not allowed in Red Cross shelters. Plan ahead for lawful storage.
In a crowd surge, do not push back - move diagonally to the edge and protect your chest.
Report threats or harassment to staff right away; call 911 for immediate danger.
proTips: Bring earplugs, an eye mask, and a small flashlight - shelters are loud and lights may stay on all night.
A cheap combination lock on a backpack zipper discourages quick theft.
Photograph your belongings and IDs before you arrive in case something goes missing.
Volunteer for a shelter task if you can; it builds friendly ties with staff and other families.
source: American Red Cross shelter guidance / CISA

sources.title: Welcome to Your Red Cross Shelter

whenNotTo: If a shelter feels unsafe and you have a safe alternative - a friend's home or hotel outside the hazard area - it is okay to go there instead.
Do not leave a shelter during an active storm or hazard to escape a minor problem; tell staff instead.

quickGlance.situation: You are staying in a public shelter or waiting in crowded aid lines after a disaster.
immediate: Keep ID, phone, cash, and medicines on your body
Never leave children alone; use the buddy system for bathrooms
Tell staff about medical needs and any safety concerns
then: In a crowd surge, move diagonally to the edge and protect your chest
Register on Red Cross Safe and Well and sign out when you leave

title: Protecting Your Identity, Documents, and Accounts in a Crisis
summary: Protect the papers and accounts you will need to prove who you are, get aid, and rebuild after a disaster - and know exactly what to do if your identity is stolen.

steps.title: Gather your critical documents
steps.body: Collect the papers you would need to prove identity, ownership, and coverage. Identification: birth, marriage, divorce, adoption, and custody records, passports, driver's licenses, Social Security cards, green cards, military IDs, and pet records. Financial and legal: deeds or leases, vehicle titles and registration, account numbers, insurance policies, tax returns, wills, trusts, and powers of attorney. Medical: insurance cards, medication and allergy lists, advance directives, and doctor contacts. Add a household inventory with photos of valuables and a list of emergency contacts.

steps.title: Store paper copies safely
steps.body: Keep originals in a fireproof and waterproof box or safe at home, in a bank safe deposit box, or with a trusted relative outside your area. If you use a safe deposit box, check who can get into it if you die or become unable to act. Keep a set of copies in a waterproof pouch in your go bag. Store home safes and boxes above flood level, not in a basement. Do not carry your Social Security card every day; keep it locked up.

steps.title: Make encrypted digital backups
steps.body: Scan or photograph every document. Store the files on a password-protected, encrypted flash drive or external drive kept in your fireproof box, and also in a secure cloud service with a strong unique password and two-step verification turned on. That way, if your home is lost and your phone is broken, you can still reach your files from any computer. Update the backup once a year and after big changes like a new car, a move, or a new insurance policy.

steps.title: Lock down your accounts
steps.body: Use a different strong password for email, banking, and government accounts, and keep them in a password manager. Turn on two-step verification, and set up a backup method in case your phone is lost - such as backup codes printed and stored with your documents. Your email is the key to every other account, so protect it most. Write your bank and card companies' fraud phone numbers on paper. Set up account alerts for large charges and logins from new devices.

steps.title: Freeze your credit - it is free
steps.body: Since 2018, federal law makes credit freezes free at all three nationwide credit bureaus: Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion. A freeze stops new accounts from being opened in your name and stays until you lift it. You must place it with each bureau separately. Requests online or by phone take effect within one business day, and you can lift a freeze within an hour when you need credit. Parents can also freeze credit for children under 16. A freeze is one of the strongest, cheapest protections there is.

steps.title: Know the difference: fraud alert vs. freeze
steps.body: A fraud alert tells lenders to verify your identity before opening credit. It is free, lasts one year, and you only need to contact one bureau, which must tell the other two. Identity theft victims can get an extended alert that lasts seven years. Service members can place an active duty alert. A fraud alert is quicker to set up after a disaster or lost wallet; a freeze is stronger. Many people use both.

steps.title: If your identity is stolen
steps.body: Act right away. Call the fraud departments of any company where fraud happened, close or freeze those accounts, and change passwords and PINs. Place a fraud alert. Get your free credit reports at annualcreditreport.com and look for accounts you do not recognize. Report the theft at IdentityTheft.gov; it creates an official Identity Theft Report and a step-by-step recovery plan with pre-filled letters. File a police report if a company requires one or you know who did it. Keep a log of every call and copies of every letter.

warnings: Never give your Social Security number, bank details, or passwords to someone who contacts you out of the blue, even if they claim to be FEMA or your bank. Verify first.
A safe deposit box may be hard to reach right after a disaster. Keep a copy set somewhere else too.
Do not store your only digital backup on the same phone or laptop that could be lost in the disaster.
If you use IdentityTheft.gov without an account, print or save your report and plan before leaving the page - you cannot get them back later.
proTips: Freeze your credit now, before any disaster. You can lift it in minutes when you need a loan.
Keep printed backup codes for two-step verification in your document box.
Write your FEMA application number and insurance claim numbers on one card in your go bag.
Check your credit reports from all three bureaus a few times a year at annualcreditreport.com.

sources.title: Safeguard Critical Documents and Valuables
sources.publisher: America's PrepareAthon! / Ready.gov (via Culver City Fire Dept.)

sources.title: Beware of Fraud and Scams (fact sheet)

whenNotTo: If you plan to apply for a loan, lease, or new phone soon, remember to temporarily lift your freeze first.
Do not email unencrypted copies of your Social Security card or passport to yourself as your only backup.

quickGlance.situation: You want your identity, documents, and accounts to survive a disaster - or you think your identity was stolen.
immediate: Put originals in a fireproof, waterproof box and copies in your go bag
Make an encrypted digital backup plus a secure cloud copy
Freeze your credit free at Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion
then: Turn on two-step verification and print backup codes
If stolen: fraud alert, check credit reports, report at IdentityTheft.gov

title: Rally Points and Lost Person Protocol
summary: Agree on meeting places and a simple 'what to do if we get separated' plan before an emergency, so a separation in a crowd, evacuation, or outdoors stays short and safe.

steps.title: Pick your meeting places now
steps.body: Choose three places everyone in the household knows. A neighborhood meeting place close to home, such as a specific neighbor's porch or the corner mailbox, for sudden events like a house fire. A regional meeting place outside your neighborhood, such as a library, place of worship, or relative's home, in case you cannot get home. And an out-of-town place for a large evacuation. Pick spots that are unmistakable, so no one pictures a different 'big tree.' Agree how long to wait at each one, for example 30 minutes at the near spot before moving to the next.

steps.title: Choose an out-of-area contact
steps.body: Pick one person who lives outside your region to be the family message hub. After a disaster, local lines jam, but calls and texts to a distant number often get through. Everyone checks in with that person, and that person passes along news. Write the number on paper for every family member, including children, because few people remember numbers stored in phones. Send texts instead of calls unless someone is in danger - texts use less network capacity and keep lines open for emergency workers.

steps.title: Brief everyone before you move
steps.body: Before any trip into a crowd, evacuation, or hike, take one minute to say the plan out loud: where we meet if separated, how long we wait, and who to call. Point to the meeting spot so children can see it. Give each child a card with their name, a parent's phone number, and the out-of-area contact. Teach children to look for a uniformed worker, a store employee at a register, or a parent with kids if they get lost, and never to leave with someone who approaches them first.

steps.title: If you are separated: STOP
steps.body: Stop moving. Think about where you last saw your group. Observe your surroundings and landmarks. Plan your next step. Outdoors, the best plan is usually to stay put in a visible spot and make noise; three whistle blasts are a widely used distress signal. Wandering usually makes you harder to find. In a city or crowd, go to the agreed meeting place by the safest route and wait the agreed time. Text your out-of-area contact your location, then save phone battery by checking every 15 to 30 minutes instead of constantly.

steps.title: If someone is missing: organize, do not scatter
steps.body: Keep the rest of the group together. One adult stays at the meeting place in case the missing person returns. Search the last known location and the most likely routes first, always in pairs - never send anyone alone. Use your voices and whistles and pause often to listen for answers. Tell nearby staff or security right away; stores, parks, and shelters have procedures for lost children. Call 911 quickly for a missing child, an older adult with dementia, or anyone lost outdoors. Searches go best when they start early, so do not wait hours hoping they will turn up.

steps.title: Reunite and update
steps.body: When you find each other, tell your out-of-area contact and anyone else searching so no one keeps looking. Talk about what went wrong and fix the plan: maybe the meeting place was hard to reach or a child did not understand. After a large disaster, you can register on the Red Cross Safe and Well site so relatives can find you. Review meeting places whenever you move, change schools or jobs, or travel somewhere new.

warnings: A meeting place no one remembers is useless. Brief children and adults before you move, not after someone is lost.
Do not send people out alone to search, especially at night. You can end up with two missing people.
Call 911 early for a missing child, a vulnerable adult, or anyone lost outdoors.
proTips: Take a photo of each child on your phone at the start of a busy day so you have their current clothing if you need to describe them.
Use landmarks that will survive the event - a brick church holds up better than a parked food truck.
Write the out-of-area contact number in permanent marker inside a child's backpack or on a wristband.
Practice with kids: at the mall, ask them to lead you to the meeting spot.
source: Ready.gov family communication plan template / Red Cross

sources.title: Family Emergency Communication Plan
sources.publisher: Oklahoma Emergency Management (Ready.gov template), hosted by NJ OEM

sources.title: Welcome to Your Red Cross Shelter

whenNotTo: Do not go to a meeting place that is now inside a hazard area - skip to the next one.
Do not delay calling 911 for a missing child to search on your own first.

quickGlance.situation: Your group got separated, or you are about to move through a crowd, evacuation, or trail.
immediate: If lost: STOP - stop, think, observe, plan
Go to the agreed meeting place and wait the agreed time
Text your out-of-area contact your location
then: Search in pairs only; keep one adult at the meeting place
Call 911 early for a missing child or vulnerable adult
